The Betrayal of the Horse: When a Horse Becomes a Verdict “This is my horse!” Mikolka cried, bringing the shaft down with a heavy blow. “Beat her to death! Why don’t you beat her?” someone shouted from the crowd. Mikolka raised the shaft again. The wretched horse collapsed on her haunches, then struggled up and tried once more to pull the cart. Six whips lashed her from every side. The shaft fell again, then again, with a terrible rhythm, as Mikolka, almost mad with rage, seemed determined to kill her in a single blow. The scene comes from Dostoevsky’s Crime and Punishment. Before Raskolnikov acts on his theory of the “extraordinary man,” he dreams of himself as a child watching a horse beaten to death. He runs to her, embraces her bloody head, kisses it, then clenches his small fists and throws himself at the man who has killed her. The dream is one of the novel’s great flashes of moral revelation. It exposes the compassion in Raskolnikov that theory has not yet destroyed. It also announces that his path will not end in the cold triumph of an idea, but in guilt, suffering, and redemption. History later produced a harsher joke. On 3 January 1889, Nietzsche is said to have seen a horse being whipped in Turin’s Piazza Carlo Alberto. According to the legend, he rushed forward in tears, threw his arms around the horse’s neck, and collapsed into madness. The story is probably apocryphal, a myth shaped after the fact, but it remains irresistible because it gives the philosopher of the Antichrist an almost Christ-like final gesture. Nietzsche, who called for the Übermensch and attacked pity as part of slave morality, is remembered as a broken man weeping over an animal. The irony is exact and cruel. The philosopher who distrusted pity is given an image of absolute pity. The voice that summoned the superman is turned into a figure of helplessness. Posterity betrayed Nietzsche by remembering him through the very kind of moral drama he would have despised. So where did the horse go? László Krasznahorkai once asked Béla Tarr that question, and the question became the origin of The Turin Horse. Tarr’s film imagines what happened after the famous Nietzsche anecdote. It takes the horse from the legend and places it in a wind-battered world of stone, mud, potatoes, silence, and extinguishing light. The problem with The Turin Horse is not its pessimism. Pessimism can still breathe. It can remain unstable, open to accident, alert to small changes in a body, a gesture, a glance, a delay. Tarr’s film is more severe than that. It turns pessimism into a verdict. Every object enters the frame already sentenced: the horse, the well, the potato, the lamp, the window, the wind. They do not move toward meaning. They have been assigned meaning in advance. Tarr begins with a horse and ends with a verdict. The animal never had a chance. That is the deepest violence of the film. The horse is introduced as body, labor, breath, muscle, resistance. In the opening carriage shot, we can still feel the animal pressing against the road, the weight of the cart, the force of the wind, the rhythm of hooves and wheels. For a moment, the horse appears as a creature caught in weather and work. It has mass. It has fatigue. It occupies the image. But almost immediately, the film begins to drain the animal of animality. The horse is no longer allowed to be hungry, stubborn, frightened, confused, irritated, exhausted in some opaque animal way. Its refusal to move cannot remain a refusal. Its silence cannot remain animal silence. Its body cannot remain a body. The horse becomes the visible form of a philosophical conclusion: the extinction of will. A horse in cinema should retain some remainder that does not translate into human meaning. It should resist us. In The Turin Horse, that remainder is crushed. The animal is not observed so much as converted. The film does not ask what a horse is. It decides what the horse must mean. Tarr’s defenders might say that this is exactly the point. The Turin Horse is not interested in the richness of ordinary life. It is interested in what remains after that richness has been stripped away. Its repetitions are not dramatic failures. They are the film’s method. The father dresses. The daughter fetches water. They eat. They look out. They sleep. The world does not develop. It diminishes. That defense is serious, but it only sharpens the problem. Even reduction can leave room for contingency. A stripped world can still surprise us. A repeated gesture can change in pressure, rhythm, tenderness, boredom, anger, fatigue. A daughter helping her father dress could disclose an entire history between them: dependence, resentment, care, old intimacy hardened into duty. Tarr gives us the action, but he seals off the variation. The repetition does not deepen life. It narrows it. The daughter dresses the father day after day, yet the ritual rarely gathers private history. It becomes another unit in the film’s machinery of depletion. Their silence is not the silence of two people who know too much to speak. It is the silence of a world emptied for metaphysical use. The potato scenes reveal the same problem. A hot potato should be one of cinema’s simplest material facts: skin, steam, fingers, hunger, salt, swallowing, disgust, impatience. Tarr films the potato with brutal attention, but the attention is strangely airless. The potato quickly ceases to be food. It becomes a survival rite, then a sign, then another confirmation that life has been reduced to endurance. The object is concrete, but its concreteness has been captured. It cannot wander away from the idea. The well runs dry in the same way. A dry well could be a practical disaster, a local mystery, an ecological fact, a social event. Here it feels like a symbolic program completing itself. The disappearance of water is not discovered. It is confirmed. The lamp that refuses to stay lit could have been a physical drama of oil, flame, wick, hand, air. Instead, the darkness arrives as an announcement the film has been preparing from the first frame. This is where the film’s images lose contingency. They look material, but they are not free. The wind is not weather. It is judgment. The window is not a window. It is a frame for waiting. The farmhouse is not quite a place. It is a metaphysical laboratory, built so that every object can be tested until it yields the same answer. Tarr’s long takes intensify this problem. They appear to grant time to things, but the time is not open. It is controlled with almost punitive precision. A long take can allow a body, a room, an animal, or a face to drift beyond interpretation. It can let duration produce accidents. In The Turin Horse, duration often does the opposite. It holds us inside a conclusion until we submit to it. We do not discover barrenness. We are instructed in it. This is why the film’s supposed return to “things themselves” feels so contradictory. If that phrase means a return to things before explanation, then The Turin Horse is in conflict with its own promise. Its objects appear with enormous physical force, yet they are never allowed to remain unstable. The horse, the well, the potato, the wind, the lamp: each arrives already bent toward the same verdict. The film does not trust things enough to let them exist without sentencing them. The contrast with Dostoevsky and Nietzsche matters because both also think through extremity. Crime and Punishment passes through murder, delirium, guilt, degradation, spiritual torment. Yet Raskolnikov is never identical with his theory. The horse in his dream tears open the system. It reveals the child who still suffers at the sight of suffering. It interrupts abstraction with pity. Nietzsche, too, is not simply a thinker of negation. Even after the death of God, his thought remains dangerous because it asks what new values might be created after collapse. The void is not only an ending. It is also a demand. However violent or unstable his answer may be, Nietzsche does not merely close the world. He hurls thought into the problem of what might come next. Tarr permits no such instability. His pessimism has no wound through which chance might enter. Every exit has been blocked before the film begins. The world is not dying in front of us. It has already been condemned, and the film spends nearly three hours making us watch the sentence carried out. That is why The Turin Horse is at once formidable and suffocating. Its craft is undeniable. Every shot is composed with terrifying discipline. Every sound seems carved into place. The wind, the footsteps, the breathing, the wooden surfaces, the silence: all of it has force. But the force serves a closed design. The film’s control is so total that life cannot surprise the image. Nothing arrives from the side. Nothing slips through the system. Nothing in the frame is permitted to escape its assigned fate. Kafka’s “A Country Doctor” offers another image of horses: irrational, sudden, terrifying, full of passage. They do not explain the world. They break it open. Tarr’s horse does the opposite. It closes the world. It does not carry us into the unknown. It stands as the completed emblem of a conclusion already reached. After nearly three hours of wind, repetition, darkness, and enforced exhaustion, the question is not whether The Turin Horse is a major work of cinematic craft. It plainly is. The question is what that craft has done to the living thing at its center. Tarr begins with a horse. A body. An animal. A creature that should have had hunger, fear, stubbornness, opacity, useless resistance. Then the film subjects it to a form so absolute that it can no longer remain alive in any unpredictable sense. The horse is not killed by Mikolka’s shaft. It is killed by meaning. The horse does not need to explain the world. It needs, at least once, to escape the meaning prepared for it.

I tried watching The Turin Horse , and I didn't get anything out of it. So I then listened to Jonathan Rosenbaum's audio commentary. hoping it might offer something I had missed. Rosenbaum talks about many things. He talks about his own relationship with Tarr, whom he calls a friend. About anecdotes from when they were in a jury together at a film festival, and they couldn't decide on a winner because Tarr hated all the films (he describes Tarr as an anti-cinephile). He describes Tarr’s shift from socio-political concerns toward something more "metaphysical" and "philosophical" from Sátántangó onward. He discusses Tarr’s collaboration with Ágnes Hranitzky, his wife and co-director, and with László Krasznahorkai, his closest collaborator, and the writer of The Turin Horse and several of Tarr's other films. Notably, what he doesn't talk about is the content of the film itself. Which is fitting, as the film offers nothing to talk about. That may be why I, too, am talking about Rosenbaum’s commentary instead of the film. --- One of the problems with films like these is that difficulty and tedium become their primary — and often only — defining characteristics. Questioning the work is then treated, by the cult of the initiated, as evidence of insufficient patience, seriousness, or artistic literacy. But art and cinema do not — and should not — earn significance merely by exhausting the viewer. Because the film itself offers remarkably little by way of internal articulation, even Rosenbaum has no choice but to turn outward: toward the director’s supposed philosophical inclinations, his biography, and Rosenbaum’s own authority as a friend of the director. If a work is so sparse that even its defenders cannot meaningfully discuss what happens within it, then the problem is not with the audience.

Oh boy. There is perhaps an argument that Béla Tarr is one of the most predictable filmmakers in contemporary cinema. The film is going to be in black and white. It’s going to feature extremely long takes. Seconds will turn into hours. Characters’ speech will sometimes sound as if they’re reading straight from an intimidating philosophical treatise or hard-line manifesto. And it’s going to be one of the grimmest things you’ve ever seen in your sorry little life. With this movie, Tarr and Hranitzky amply follow through on all of these predictive suppositions, and just to add even more spice to proceedings, there is no dialogue for the first 30 minutes. There’s a short introductory voiceover, and then…no one speaks. At all. For half an hour. Meanwhile, a string refrain that sounds like Phillip Glass’s Koyaanisqatsi score under the influence of heavy sedatives repeats over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over again. The story? A father and daughter live in a dilapidated hovel in the middle of nowhere. That’s it. That’s the whole film. I just saved you 154 minutes. Oh yeah- and it’s the windiest place in the world. This is a film that is about wind as much as it is about anything else. The wind howls. The wind whistles. It howls. It whistles. It tugs at the windows and the doors. The hovel creaks. The string refrain scrapes its way through another tortuous, hopelessly despairing iteration. The daughter helps the father get dressed in an unbroken take- there’s 10 minutes. The daughter goes to the well- let’s follow her all the way there and all the way back again as she fights her way through the ridiculous wind. There’s another 10 minutes. Even by Béla Tarr’s standards, this was extreme. It was simply one of the most challenging films I have ever watched to completion. Imagine Robert Eggers’ The Lighthouse with 95% of the dialogue taken out and being played at 20% speed. Was it an allegory? Most certainly. Do I care? No. Will I be watching it again, ever? Only after death, if I find myself in hell. For more of my reviews, why not visit www.wilfullyobtuse.com.

El caballo de Turín: Pue eso. Que lo disfruten otros. El director húngaro Bela Tarr es incompatible con mi manera de entender y disfrutar el cine. Sin embargo, las revistas especializadas le dedican páginas y páginas de admiración incondicional. Tiene su mérito. No debe de ser fácil escribir tanto, y con semejante entusiasmo, sobre la nada. El prólogo explica que Nietzsche perdió definitivamente la razón después de presenciar cómo un cochero azotaba a su caballo porque este se negaba a avanzar. Bela Tarr no se interesa por las misteriosas razones de aquella locura, sino por el cochero, su hija y el caballo. Es decir, por mostrar con una minuciosidad casi enfermiza lo que hacen durante seis días a lo largo de 146 interminables minutos. Diez minutos siguiendo un carro. Siete encerrando al caballo en la cuadra mientras arrecia una tormenta. Ocho viendo cómo el cochero se cambia de ropa al llegar a casa. Cinco contemplándolo comer una patata cocida. Otros cinco mirando cómo su hija se come la suya. Diez más con ambos observando el paisaje. Nueve acompañando al hombre mientras se desnuda antes de acostarse. Y así, una y otra vez, hasta el final. Lo juro. No es broma. Para mí es un truño importante con pretensiones líricas. Pero es que no tienes ni puta idea, Hugo. Tampoco sensibilidad artística. Puede ser. Será que mi visión del cine está muy limitada al no encontrar poesía en el aburrimiento. Ahora mismo solo tengo una necesidad y es volver a refugiarme en John Ford, Howard Hawks o Billy Wilder. Allí, al menos, siento que el cine sigue siendo sinónimo de emoción.

Revendo 14 anos depois, com uma concepção formada sobre o que acredito ser a vocação do cinema, gostei bem menos deste trabalho final de Béla Tarr. Compreendo perfeitamente as intenções contra-hegemônicas do diretor. De modo geral, ele propunha o reverso do cinema de storytelling, em que tudo se resume a "contar uma boa história", conferindo-se ao enredo uma centralidade absoluta. E, de fato, o cinema de storytelling é a décima primeira praga do Egito. Mas Tarr, embora operando no regime do cinema narrativo, suprime consideravelmente o plot, com seu arco dramático, reviravoltas, surpresas etc. É quase um retorno aos Lumière. Em uma entrevista, o húngaro disse recusar-se ao esquema de montagem corriqueiro, baseado em "informação-corte-informação-corte". Às vezes não há informação alguma, e outras vezes a informação está algures na mise-en-scène. Mas até aqui tudo bem, já que há bons exemplos de mise-en-scène rica e naturalismo ajustado ao teor da narrativa. O problema de "O Cavalo de Turim" é que ele não é apenas anti-storytelling; é anti-cinematográfico. Para além do ascetismo à Bresson, com personagens cujos pensamentos e emoções são inescrutáveis, já que tudo que vemos são exterioridades distanciadas e economia expressiva, aplica-se a lógica documental ao material ficcional: longos planos-cena e raríssimos cortes, profundidade de campo e reprodução fotográfica do visível ao invés de sua transfiguração. Até existe uma narratividade mínima, onde pouco a pouco, em meio ao marasmo cotidiano, vemos algumas mudanças. Mas elas não são inseridas para catalisar a narrativa, voltá-la noutra direção, alterar objetivos de personagens, nada disso. Se assim fosse, poderíamos tentar examinar se a forma "documental" se justificaria em face delas. Entretanto, o que parece interessar ao diretor é simplesmente o contraste entre o vazio existencial da gente simples de Turim no fim do séc. XIX com a agudeza intelectual de Nietzsche, que passou naquele lugar seus últimos anos. Mas note o seguinte: não temos nenhum vislumbre deste na obra. É para o camponês, sua filha e o cavalo que Tarr direciona as câmeras, Ora, a encenação de um único incidente – aquele em que o filósofo alemão defende o cavalo do impiedoso açoite do camponês – até acentuaria tal contraste e justificaria o roteiro. Mas este não é um filme de "incidentes".

Couldn't finish this. It's clearly an unbelievable film in terms of craft but I can't stand it when I get the message after fifteen minutes and realise there's nothing more to it. I understand that we're grounded in this banal phenomenology to convey nihilism. Even the very existence of the film being about the horse that drove Nietzsche insane is itself a meta commentary on idols and myth, which is then dispelled in the most haunting manner. But I just found it to be frustrating. I'd genuinely rather just read Nietzsche! - who does happen to be probably my favourite philosopher as well. I don't really understand what the purpose of forcing someone into endurance serves exactly. It almost feels insulting to the audience's intelligence to force us to inhabit pure nihilism through repetition. This to me is a classic example of an artwork that ceases to be interesting past the concept, and once you understand the concept and realise there's 140 minutes left of that same idea, you get tired very fast. Perhaps the only moment I found truly compelling was the person buying brandy who delivered the Nietzschean style monologue. But even then, I found this frustrating because it means this a film that exercises restraint to the nth degree and then punctuates that with such explicatory blocks of speech, that it almost feels insecure to me. Like just in case you didn't work out that this film is about nihilism, we'll have a five minute long monologue just to reiterate the point. In an alternate universe, I'm a cinephile who can endure films like these. In this current physical incarnation, I am not one of these people.

Nietzschean nihilism is a ground zero of nothingness. The lethargic decadence of once elite history makers allows for the virulent power grab of outside forces, that then deterritorialize the structures of society. This film hones in on the former (nothingness, zero, pure the dread of pure potentiality) while giving us only a glimpse of the latter (the takeover of the other), even though one cannot be without the other. I come away from this thinking there are two possible reasons for this decision by the filmmaker. Either: 1) he doesn’t fully grasp the dynamic nature of Nietzsche’s thought or 2) he focuses on nothingness because it gives him a reason to make a drab and slow movie. Maybe it’s a little bit of both, but either way, the idea here is secondary to the technique. And that for me is a disingenuous way to make a movie. You don’t make slow, motionless films because you want to make one, you make it because it’s a way to convey something. The cart is before the horse; this man just wants to show us he has the capacity to make a long, slow movie. A massive waste of time.

Kızına bakışı bile sevgi yerine hala iş görüyor mu diye kontrol eder gibi. Her gün aynı döngü uyan, giydir, içki, at, patates ye, camdan bak. At yürümüyor hayat ilerlemiyor ve hem açlar hem de patatesi yemiyorlar yani yaşamak için fiziksel sebep olsada anlam yok. Filmde bu noktaya kadar sahiplik, değer ve anlam tamamen işlev üzerinden kurulmuş. Buraya kadar güzel ama takıldığım yer de tam bu. Film sürekli “her şey değersizleşti, insan içten içe öldü” diyor ama baştan gösterdiği canlı bir değer, tutunulacak bir anlam hiç yok ki yıkımını hissedelim. Karakterlerle bağ kurmak zaten mümkün değil çünkü ortada karakter yok sadece hareket eden bedenler var. Ne hissediyorlar, neyin yasını tutuyorlar, neden yaşıyorla. hiçbir şey açılmıyor. Çöküşü izliyoruz ama çöken bir hayat görmediğimiz için etkisi de olmuyor. Başından beri bitmiş bir dünyayı altı kez tekrar izlemek gibi. At yemiyor, kuyu kuruyor, ışık gidiyor. Bunlar büyük metaforlar gibi girip bırakiyor. Sadece “bak her şey sönüyor” diyor. Eee tamam sönüyor da bu bana ne düşündürüyor? İzleyiciye alan açmakla hiçbir şey kurmamak arasında fark var, bunda ikincisi var. Zaten en başından beri hayat mekanik bir tekrar. Dolayısıyla yok oluş bir çöküş gibi değil uzatılmış bir hiçlik gibi. Tempo meselesine gelirsem evet uzun planlar düşünmek için alan açıyor ama bir noktadan sonra aynı şeyi defalarca izlemek derinlikten çok durağanlık hissi yaratmış. Hareketsizlik de bilinçli bir tercih evet ama bu kadar da amaçsızlık izleyiciyle kurulan bağı zorlamış. Tanrı meselesi de çok kararsız. La película empieza poderosa, en medio de la tempestad, un hombre con su caballo intentando que el viento no se los lleve, una música ensordecedora y te meten una cita de Nietzsche en una transición igual de magnífica que el comienzo. Esos son los primeros cinco minutos de película, parecía pometedor y luego ves al hombre entrando en su rutina, se mete a casa y... empiezan a comer papas. Toda la película es un hombre levantándose de la cama, comiendo papas y volviéndose a acostar. Hay un trecho enorme de la película donde el hombre solo se la pasa comiéndose unas malditas papas. No pasa nada, no pasa más nada. Bien, me quieres vender la cotidianidad, pero, ¿me tenías que hacerme tragar la rutina de varios días del mismo hombre comiéndose unas papas? Más o menos a mitad de película llega un sujeto a la casa y dije: finalmente se dignaron a que pasara algo. Pero no, el sujeto era una herramienta al espectador para darnos contexto de toda la situación, pero la actuación es pobre y es una inmediata verborrea con toques líricos y poco destellos narrativos. Ahí dije: suficiente. No pude seguir viendo más, sé que pasa algo al final, pero no importa. Creo que estamos acostumbrados a que pase algo, sé que el director es así, la otra vez hizo tragarme 15 minutos de una persona caminando, pero la película duraba sus seis horas, quince minutos eran un pestañeo, pero aquí... esa grandilocuencia del inicio no se concreta con el hombre comiendo papas y menos con ese final que pareciera más el empate del inicio. Perfectamente la película se pudo haber terminado con el hombre comiendo papas y hubiese sido la misma basura. Decepcionante, aburrida y muy pobremente escrita. Que no se me malentienda, amo el cine somnífero, pero hay límites que simplemente no se pueden cruzar.

I dip into slow cinema once every six months to challenge myself by going out of my comfort zone but this is my last detour in my journey to watch all of film canon. A father and daughter survive a storm which could be interesting if it was an hour shorter. There are only so many ways you could show a man peeling a potato before you send the audience running back to their phones. More than the slow pace I am bothered by the lack of narrative. I have mentioned in other reviews – The decision to let the visuals do the heavy lifting does not work for me in spite of some beautiful, painterly images. Cinema is not just a visual medium it is a visual storytelling medium. That is not a difference in semantics but in function. The slow pace is an invitation to think but the movie does not give me much food for thought. Arthouse films peaked in the 60s with the likes of Fellini, Bergman, Antonioni and Rohmer. All of them are on the slower side but they ask incisive questions about sex, religion and creativity. They reward thinking you have to ponder about the character motivation to get most out of them. On the other hand slow cinema from directors like Tarr, Claire Denis or Abbas Kiarostami has one-note characters who never give the impression of having rich inner lives so thinking about them adds nothing to the experience. They are just badly paced, thematically empty and unabashedly self-indulgent. I am not fond of either extremes – I hate both Fast and Furious and its ilk, and slow cinema. Neither has any semblance of story and to enjoy them one has to either stop thinking or give into overthinking.

If I hadn't watched Damnation or Werckmeister harmonies I would've been tempted to rate this higher for fear of 'not getting it' and being too ADHD for trve art ©️. But I did watch them, and I loved them, and I did not love this. Bella Tarr surprisingly *underestimates* himself here by putting the audience in a trance in the first 20 minutes, and then totally forgot about doing anything with the spell for the next 2 hours. There are genuinely gut wrenching and excruciatingly beautiful moments in this movie, in fact it opens with one of the most affectionate portrayals of the man-horse relationship you'll ever see. And you probably will never look at potatoes the same after this. But, and it's a big but, you don't need an eternity to explain the monotonous and simple headed life of rural farmhands, or make use tear up over animal suffering or female semi-illiteracy or delirium tremons. In fact if you view art as a medium for eliciting emotional responses - putting the viewer is a coma is not a great idea at all. By the time the drama does happen, or the narrator(s?) wax philosophical about the metaphor of decay with post-enlightement civilisation or whatever, the whole thing becomes tainted by your expectation for pay off. And it's not one of those things like Wages of Fear or whatever where your expectations being met or not are part of the aesthetic enjoyment later on. With this particular movie, nobody will feel that they're glad to have got through it outside of simply proving to themselves that they have the stomach for auteur cinema. Boredom and pacing aside, let's talk about the content itself... it's really actually quite confused with itself, and I just assume the trance is the only thing that stops someone from noticing. I mean ever since Aristotle it's understood that art in general follows the pattern of X is to Y what Y is to Z, the metaphor. Obviously, that's an overly simple box - but it's effectively ubiquitous in all good art. So what's the metaphor here? well that's not even difficult to figure out at all... a man walks in towards the halfway mark of the movie and literally tells us that the natural disaster occuring is because of exactly which metaphorical reasons and then in case there was any mystery about it all you see the exact literal non metaphor evidenced in the most unimaginative way both visually and with a soothing narrator telling you exactly what's happening. no thank you at all, the world is not any better for this movie, except for making me appreciate how difficult life is for amputees and also appreciating the silent suffering of women and horses more. Which i had felt in about 20 minutes of the movie anyways.

In other contexts at least - usually Asian. So I’m hanging out with Bela Tarr again to test my cineaste bonafides, and it’s slightly better this time, but still not for me. A father and daughter living in a small shack in the countryside is subject to unexplained misfortunes - they wake up one day and their well has dried up. The horse stops eating and working. Apocalypse surrounds them, as gales howl, and it appears that nature is abandoning them, humble as their life is. It’s all shot in this transcendent style, with long takes and slow moving cameras, and a beautifully deliberate use of zooms and framing. The black and white photography is lovely. The glacial pace is arguably appropriate in depicting this slow death of a family. Trust me, I get it. It’s just not particularly enjoyable, edifying, or enlightening. Only in small moments do the images suck you in to a point of flow. You’re never out of analysis mode. (When we observe the cart outside the house, we know in advance that Tarr is going to make us watch the entire thing be unloaded). If there’s a lack on my part, I guess that it’s not because I don’t understand it, or that I’m a Tik-Tok-addled millennial, but I’m simply not at a level of Zen not to let thought take over in the long scenes of people eating potatoes. Olha… The Turin Horse é aquele tipo de filme que você respeita mais do que gosta. Dirigido por Béla Tarr, ele tem uma proposta claramente artística e até fascinante em teoria, mas na prática, pode ser extremamente cansativo. A rotina repetitiva do pai e da filha, comendo batata e encarando o vento infinito, até funciona como metáfora no começo. Você entende a ideia: o esgotamento da vida, o peso da existência, o mundo “apagando”. Só que chega um ponto em que o filme parece preso nessa mesma repetição e não evolui o suficiente pra sustentar o interesse. Visualmente, o filme é lindo. O preto e branco, os planos longos, a atmosfera pesada… tudo muito bem construído. Mas ao mesmo tempo, o ritmo é tão arrastado que acaba afastando mais do que envolvendo. "El caballo de Turín" es un relato surgido a partir de una vivencia de Nietzsche. La anécdota relata como este filosofo, luego de observar el maltrato de un cochero hacia su caballo, se abraza al animal sollozando para luego caer en una depresión, posterior alienación y por ultimo, fallecimiento. Aquella anécdota, que es fundamental, reimagina la vida de este cochero a quien la película vuelve protagonista para que lo acompañemos, junto a su hija, durante los seis días que dura una especie de tormenta de viento. La película cruza el umbral de la contemplación hacia una extensa filmación de la vida que estos personajes llevan, haciéndonos parte de esa rutina y volviéndolo un hastío para quien lo ve. Una rutina en la que no hay recuerdo de algo mejor, de cuando hubo algo de cariño, o por lo menos de melancolía. Es un mundo que cualquiera que lo vea preferiría que terminase en vez de perpetuarlo. Está numerada la hazaña de los treinta largos planos. También lo majestuoso que esconde filmar una puerta por quince segundos después que ha sido cerrada, o las varias  veces que comen papas hervidas. Las notas son las mismas que toca Nietzsche cuando dice que "Dios ha muerto", enunciado que en la película parecía subtextual hasta la aparición de un personaje que, monologo mediante, lo eleva a la superficie del guion y toda esa lentitud, contemplación y tristeza que sigue ahora parece ya redundante. Seré un espectador no cualificado para ver la genialidad de la película, pero creo que es demasiado literal, minimalista y fatalista, por lo menos, para mi gusto.

To quote one of my favorite Community episodes: "Unfortunately for [Bela Tarr] and millions of [directors] like [him], just because something is in black and white doesn't mean it's good." You know these memes where it's like "Film bros when you tell them your favorite film is Avengers and not a 5 hour long black&white film from 1956 about the horrors of war as told through the perspective of a pidgeon"? This is it, this is the film those people are making fun of. This really feels like Bela Tarr saw Jeanne Dielman and Au Hasard Balthazar and thought to himself: "I want to make something like this, but considerably worse." This was my first introduction to Tarr and if his other films are anything like this, I don't think I'll even bother. I mean, I have nothing against slow films where nothing happens, if you need proof, just read my Jeanne Dielman review, but Turin Horse just has literally nothing to offer. No atmosphere, no emotions, no new insights into the world at large or anything like that, which you would expect from a film hailed as an arthouse masterpiece. The film is completely up its own ass, the definition of style over substance. And you wanna know what's funny about that? It doesn't even look *that* good. I mean, sure, it has some nice shots, but it's not nearly beautiful enough to warrent this lack of substance. I wouldn't say it's a bad film though. It has some decent ideas like how the family slowly loses the things that are important for their survival. Despite making fun of how the film looks, there are also a handful of geniuenly great shots in here every now and then, they just get overshadowed by all the not-so-great ones that make up a majority of the film. The music is also a big plus, although its very over-used. Maybe I was just in the wrong mood, or maybe there's really something about this that I "just don't get", but I felt completely empty during the entire runtime and afterwards. And I don't mean that feeling of emptiness that you get after a great film, I mean that feeling of emptiness that you get when you order cavier and realize you just paid like 100 bucks for some lightly salted slimeballs.

The Turin Horse stands as an unapologetic, uncompromising monument to apocalyptic nihilism. Opening with the famous anecdote of Friedrich Nietzsche’s mental collapse after witnessing a cabman whip a stubborn horse in Turin, the film shifts its gaze away from the philosopher to focus instead on the horse, its aging owner, and his daughter. Over six days, Béla Tarr meticulously tracks the slow, relentless unraveling of their basic existence. Shot in stark monochrome, the film is a mesmerizing work of pure atmosphere—its hypnotic rhythm and austere visuals immersing viewers in a vision of existential collapse. Unyielding in its artistic conviction, The Turin Horse offers a rare, uncompromising meditation on the futility of human struggle. It is a work that will resonate deeply with purists of extreme slow cinema, commanding respect for its bleak beauty and unwavering dedication to form.

Le cheval de Turin est plus une expérience qu’un film comme on a l’habitude de voir Ce film nous parle de la fin, plus qu’une sorte de fin du monde, oui, une réelle fin au sens large, le dernier film de Béla Tarr, la fin de sa carrière, son dernier message au monde jugeant qu’il n’aurait plus rien à dire après. En me renseignant j’ai appris que les plans séquences étaient sa spécialité et oui, bon sang que le film en est rempli, souvent d’une durée de 3 minutes, 3 longues minutes, et pendant ces 3 minutes ce que nous voyons ? Du noir et du blanc, c’est la lividité de ce monde touchant à son terme, c’est ça que nous voyons et nous y assistons péniblement, car oui, pénible est le quotidien du viel agriculteur et de sa fille dont nous n’arriverons pas à nous souvenir du nom. Il est également intéressant de noter que le cheval de Turin est à l’origine, comme raconté en voix off au début du film, une histoire présumée vraie où Friedrich Nietzsche en voyage à Turin, aurait aperçut un cheval de faisait molester par un cocher et se serait interposé entre le cheval et le fouet accablé par la situation, il aurait par le suite viré à la démence et aurait finis sa vie dans cet état. Malgré le fait que je ne le regarderai sûrement pas une seconde fois, je sens que je vais me souvenir de ce film pendant longtemps, chaque plan aussi long et ennuyant soit-il, nous donne l’impression que nous assistons tout de même à quelque chose de grand, je pourrais mettre pause à n’importe quel moment du film et avoir l’impression de contempler une ancienne peinture d’une beauté et d’une profondeur qui donnerai bon nombre d’analyse de nos jours, oui, Le cheval de Turin est un film atmosphérique et contemplatif qui nous offre l’expérience de contempler la fin d’un monde sans dieu.

A fine example of slow cinema. And by slow I mean slowly descending into unmitigated dread and despair. This film had a constant feeling of impending doom. From the black and white world in which a disabled father and his dutiful daughter live out their lives in complete and utter monotony. But it’s like the worst kind of monotony, where every day is a struggle to survive. Boiled potatoes, waterless well, sick horse. The cacophony of unending wind contrasted with the minimal dialogue script and isolated environment made the film feel weirdly claustrophobic. Pair that with the repetitive music score, or rather a lullaby from hell, the film never let up on making me feel completely uncomfortable throughout. This film was like a combination of a Tarkovsky and Lynchian nightmare, all wrapped into an existential psychotic episode of depression and nihilism.

Watching a man and his daughter eat the same boiled potato every night for six days shouldn't be riveting and somehow it was, or at least riveting in the strange, hypnotic way that staring at a fire is riveting. There's barely a plot, a farmer and his adult daughter live in a windswept shack with their horse, who one day simply refuses to work anymore, and from there the days repeat with only small variations, fetching water, getting dressed with one good arm, staring out at the endless wind battering their home. That repetition is the entire point, and it took me a while to stop fighting it, to stop waiting for some narrative development that Tarr clearly has no intention of providing. Once I gave in, the accumulation of these identical days started to feel less like tedium and more like watching entropy itself, the slow grinding down of two lives until even the well runs dry and the lamp refuses to stay lit. The cinematography does an enormous amount of quiet work, long handheld takes that follow these characters through their shack with a patience that borders on reverence, camera drifting past details, worn hands, cracked walls, that constant howling wind on the soundtrack, never letting you forget how hostile the world outside has become. Mihaly Vig's score returns again and again, this mournful, circling melody that starts to feel less like music and more like the wind's own voice given shape. There's a visitor midway through who delivers this bitter monologue about the collapse of meaning in the world, and it's the only real burst of language in the entire film, landing with startling weight precisely because everything around it has been so quiet. I won't claim this was an easy sit, entire stretches challenge you to just endure alongside these two, and I understand completely why people walk out. But by the time the lamp finally goes dark for good, I felt like I'd witnessed something closer to a ritual than a story, and its bleakness has stayed lodged in me since.

The Turin Horse is certainly a bit of an endurance test of a film; with the plot kept to a minimum,  Bela Tarr made a very ambitious two and a half hour project that’s made entirely out of twelve extended takes, which has the effect of letting real life go on in real time, what would usually be cut or consisted not important enough to film made the focus here. Set on a remote farm, we get to see the everyday struggles in this life, working hard repetitive labour that doesn’t let you as a viewer get out of it either. You’ve got to almost admire Tarr sticking to his vision so unwaveringly, though on some level his film is almost a textbook example (or caricature) of a slow, arty international movie, and after a slightly different opening really just locks into one location. It takes a fair bit of commitment from you as the audience, a couple of times in the second half I thought it was going to end before everything suddenly jumped forward to a new day just when this seemed to be wrapping up. It might be the Stockholm syndrome talking, though, but even when this is a bit of a task to sit and watch for something deliberately stripped down it does draw you in. Tarr’s bleakly beautiful imagery challenges itself to narrow down the broad human experience to 2 people, each new loop or new slightly different way of showing the same daily grind just really showing the control he has over the form here. With the help of really vivid sound design, he creates  a soundscape that makes everything feel like it’s been made on an alien planet,  something almost apocalyptic here that bubbles up as it goes along. It’s one meant to be heavy and slow, although making everything a metaphor means like the hot potato the farmer handles there’s ultimately less to unwrap in the long run while you’re actually watching. With images that so stick in your head, and a committed push for the “real” to almost unnerving places, it’s impressive how much this locks in and commits to its bleak, elliptical story, definitely an experience even if while watching I was often champing at the bit for this to have a little more to it.

Béla Tarr ne cherche pas à raconter une histoire mais à faire ressentir une fin, une extinction lente, silencieuse, sans explication. C’est un film difficile à commenter parce qu’il refuse le discours : on ne le comprend pas vraiment, on le subit.

Tak jak śmierć Davida Lyncha w zeszłym roku zmotywowała mnie do nadrobienia jego filmografii, tak odejście Béla Tarra sprawiło, że postanowiłem obejrzeć "Koń turyński". Niestety nie znalazłem wielu innych jego dzieł z polskimi napisami. Koń, którego niegdyś Nietzsche ocalił przed cierpieniem ze strony woźnicy, zaczyna niedomagać - odmawia jedzenia i pracy. Film opowiada też historię woźnicy i jego córki. Zdziwiłem się, że opowieść László Krasznahorkaia, którą obecnie czytam, stała się zaczątkiem dla ostatniego filmu węgierskiego mistrza kina. To było bardzo długie, 155 minut mojego życia. Nie jestem pewien, czy to nie był najmniej dynamiczny seans, jaki widziałem. Musiałem obejrzeć go w dwóch częściach, bo za pierwszym razem zasnąłem. Dlatego wydaje mi się, że próg wejścia jest bardzo wysoki dla przeciętnego widza. Ja ledwo przez niego przebrnąłem. To ponury, surowy i smutny obraz o wyraźnie apokaliptycznym klimacie. Jednocześnie urzekły mnie zdjęcia Freda Kelemena. Bohaterowie wykonują codziennie te same czynności, popadają w rutynę. Prawdopodobnie na długo zapamiętam odgłos wiatru, który towarzyszy nam niemal cały czas. Z jednej strony było to mocne, niezwykle pesymistyczne doświadczenie, w którym przez sześć dni świat powoli się kończy. Z drugiej, nie był to najciekawszy seans w moim życiu. The Turin Horse takes its’ place along with Jeanne Dielman among the greatest “potato” films of all time.😀 This is my first Bela Tarr and now I’m afraid that I might end up going down a Tarr rabbit hole, if for no other reason than seeing if his other works are as unyielding a parade of stark, painterly images. The opening shot is over five minutes long and it is of an old horse ( no indication if it’s from Turin ) pulling a wagon. The camera is directly in front of the horse giving the viewer an intense experience of the horse’s suffering. This film is shot in Black&White and it is amazing to look at, even though Tarr holds on shots for a while. The story involves a farmer & his daughter in Hungary..maybe. The “where” isn’t clear . Also not clear..the “when”. This might be set in 1890 or 1940 or 1962?! The technology presented is possibly post-Industrial Revolution but even then there is a lack of items of any sort of modernity. They use well water, they eat with their hands,  there’s no electricity; their homestead is isolated. It’s far away from everything. The only thing around for miles is the unrelenting wind. Cruel, cruel nature. I mentioned Chantal Ackerman’s Jeanne Dielman at the beginning and these films share more than potatoes. They depict an adherence to routine that is necessary for the survival of the body but also the survival of the Psyches of their protagonists. Another common element is that they are both broken into days. If I recall properly, Jeanne Dielman takes place over three days and this film counts off six days. Six days of eating and not finishing two potatoes. Six days of fetching two pails of water and Six days trying to get their horse to move. This isolation is broken twice. Once by a neighbor that has traveled a great distance to buy a bottle of brandy (the old man makes brandy🤷🏼‍♂️) and apparently to monologue obliquely about facism, capitalism, oligarchs etc. This reminded me of another film; Tarkovsky’s The Sacrifice. That film depicts a more modern family that is also weirdly cut off from the world in which an alluded to, far away conflict seems to be seeping into their reality; a conflict that is unnamed with unnamed combatants. After this interaction, there is more desolation. The wind continues to howl and the horse refuses to eat, drink or move. It feels like the horse is signaling its impending death..maybe their death, too. The 2nd interaction is with a wagon full of folks described as Gypsies. They arrive with laughing, shambolic menace. The daughter confronts them as they begin to take water from the well. They taunt and paw at the daughter and we begin to feel that this is going to turn out horribly but the farmer comes out of the house with a hatchet and that’s enough to cause the Gypsies to move on. I’ll say this, they might represent chaos and criminality but they’re the only ones with smiles. Not too long after the Gypsies leave..the well runs dry. I have to sidebar about the weird way they eat these potatoes. The daughter peels two taters, one for each of them. They eat them by hand. They peel these scalding potatoes with their fingernails. The father, who only has the use of his left hand, smashes the potato by slamming his good hand into it. They also never seem to finish the potatoes. They’re hungry but also sick of eating the potatoes..I can see it. This left-handedness of the father and the abject desolation they’re experiencing made me wonder if Tarr wants us to consider the possibility that this story is purposefully reminiscent of a fable in which the old man made a “deal with the devil”. It’s something to consider. There is no real conclusion or resolution and I didn’t find that frustrating but this movie is 2 hours and 15 minutes so it’s kind of a long way to go to leave us where we started, worrying about that poor horse. A film nem tartalom, hanem morális állásfoglalás. Tarr élete során ezt az elvet követte. Ez talán ebben, az utolsó filmjében mutatkozik meg igazán. Ahogy a Partizán potcastben is elmondta, a filmművésznek el kell döntenie hogy művészet marad, vagy inkább a szórakoztató ipar részévé válik. Hogy cgi szuperhősöket akarunk nézni, vagy kulturálódni. Tarr mindog a művészet mellé tette le a voksát, és talán itt éreztem ezt a legjobban. Nem fogok hazudni, ezt a filmet fájdalmas volt végignézni, az utolsó fél órára már elfáradtam, és ezt úgy mondom hpgy Tart Béla az egyik kedvenc rendezőm. Ez a film két és fél óra semmi. Béla szavaival élve "kozmikus semmi". És ez nem egy rossz dolog! Nem kell elvárnunk egy filmtől hogy kiszolgáljon, hogy szórakoztasson. Ez a film gondolkozásra késztet. Gondolkodsz közben, de nem más dolgolról, hanem a filmmel együtt gondolkozol. Amiket mi látunk ebben a filmben azok véglények. Ez nem élet. Ez életben maradás. Élet ez egyáltalán? Nem. Ez csak létezés. A motorikus képességeik tartják őket életben, rutinból élnek. "Sokan 25 évesen meghalnak, de csak 75 évesen temetik el őket"- Benjamin Franklin Ppntosan ugyan ezt látjuk. Ők csak léteznek, de nem élnek. Főleg az apuka, a lányban maradt még egy csepp, ő törődik a lóval, nem csak a saját életbenmaradásához szolgaló ezközként tekint rá. Ebben a filmben ha egy szó se lenne, az se lenne baj. Ahogy az apuka kapkod a krumplihoz, gyorsan leszedi a bőrét, összezúzza és gyordan befalj miközben levegőt vesz hogy hűljön, mindent elárul. Ez nem étkezés, ez táplálkozás. Csakis életbenmaradásról szól. A lány viszont fogja a krumplit. Itt látszódnak az apró különbségek. Azt hiszem ez történik ma kicsiben minden emberrel. Tarr látott mindent.

Canto de cisne del gran realizador y maestro húngaro, última obra formal de ficción con la cual anunció su retiro –mismo que terminó siendo parcial pues en 2019 presentaría Missing People, una incrustación al cine extendido a manera de  documental/instalación a solicitud expresa del Wiener Festwochen Festival de Viena– una brutal epístola de partida en la que encumbre y reviste con profundidad y parsimonia (cual fue su costumbre) los temas y acercamientos existenciales que manejó durante su filmografía; cruenta esquela que en su afonía y sosiego explora el devenir humano y su efímero y encarnizado paso por la experiencia de la vida. En esta edificación la contemplación y el silencio se presentan portentosamente como un retablo de los tiempos universales, no marcando o caracterizando una época o un tiempo (o región), sino que perfilan y definen nuestra propia naturaleza. El propio Tarr llegó a mencionar sobre esta, su última impresión, que trataba sobre la pesadez de la existencia humana. Basada en la ya mítica anécdota donde Friedrich Nietzsche defiende a un caballo de feroces azotes y que, según el consenso general, marca el preámbulo de su hundimiento mental; esta postal que increpa el origen del filme mantiene a su vez una inquietante relación con un paraje de la excelsa Crimen y Castigo de Fiódor Dostoyevski (publicada apenas un par de décadas atrás); donde el protagonista Rodion Raskólnikov se sueña de niño viendo como es violentamente golpeado un caballo, como él lo intenta defender con todas sus fuerzas sobre un llanto profundo, pero al final todo resulta inútil. Sumando una capa más a este soporte discursivo que dialoga entre memorias históricas e interpretaciones ontológicas y morales, Béla Tarr se apoya de László Krasznahorkai (Nobel de Literatura 2025) –quien no le es nada ajeno; adaptó algunas de sus novelas como también colaboró directamente con él en otros guiones– para acoger la peripecia ya afamada y sortear el camino más común: el hombre (el sabio, el ilustrado), y así poder enfocarse en un lindante temático de la misma importancia: el caballo. De esta forma, siguiendo al vejado jamelgo es como la trama nos lleva a un acampado solitario –y que en parte nos recuerda al mejor  Bergman– para así cercanos en linderos de apatía, en un confinamiento que intenta ser rutinario pero que pronto habrá de develar la decadencia del todo. El recorrido trazado es el de una agonía, pero su tratamiento no es apuntalado en lo agónico, es en cambio en el de la quietud; un dolor que abraza y se acepta cual destino. No es que no se pueda luchar contra él, es tan sólo que es ese el punto común donde todos habremos de encontrarnos finiquitados; allanados en un mutismo voraz que nos explica y nos despliega. Le inexistencia como parte de. El Caballo de Turín de Béla Tarr parte, entonces, de una nota al pie de la filosofía y rompe las membranas de las horas y los años, de los segundos y los lustros. Se anida en la promesa de un pozo siempre proveedor y se enfrenta a un viento sempiterno que devela al agotamiento al tiempo que anuncia el borde y el corolario. Es una venta atroz pero sincera. La voz con que Béla Tarr construye –y construyó– su despedida es apenas audible, es sutil, pero tiene una potencia enorme: un agreste campo, perturbador como sugestivo donde la turbación y la calma no se disputan o enemistan sino simplemente se dan la mano.

On January 3rd 1889, renowned German philosopher Fredrich Nietzsche acted in opposition to the very philosophy he had spent the entireity of his adult life preaching. Upon witnessing the brutal whipping of a horse in Turin by a carriage driver, overwhlmed by empathy and sadness, he rushed over to the aforementioned horse and hugged it, preventing it being beat any longer. He sobbed greatly and was eventually removed by a friend of his, and transported back to his quarters, where he would remain in a delirious sleep-state for 2 days. This marked his profound mental breakdown, under which he would remain for the next 10 years of his life, cared for by his mother and his family before his eventual passing. Tarr begins The Turin Horse with a narration that essentially summarises these events. Yet, Tarr's introduction also ends with the line "yet no one knows what happened to the horse." That is the story that Tarr wants to tell, the story of the horse after this infamous incident. Bela Tarr's The Turin Horse is an apocalyptic tale of death. Not just the death of human or animal life, but the death of life itself, in a profoundly existential way, life as a force itself. We follow this family of two, a father and a daughter, as they carry out their monotonous daily routines, repeated over 6 days. Their lives are spent mostly in silence, the two hardly involve themselves in many conversations with each other, and they carry on with a deep resignation. A resignation of life, of meaning and an eventual submission to suffering and death. It is one of the bleakest narratives I have seen; a completely painful experience as the inevitability of death and meaninglessnes takes over, a complete dissolution of the human spirit. I will not claim to know or have read much of Nietzche's works, but it's clear Tarr employs Nietzsche as more than just a narrative prologue to the begin his story. He turns Nietzsche's concepts of nihilism and stasis into a daily routine for these protagonists, mirroring the empty hopelessness of their lives. The repetitive sequences mirror his idea of eternal reccurrence. I'm sure there's even more meaning that I may not have picked up in relation to Nietzsche's philosophy because of my lack of having read his work, but what all I could pick up is extremely alluring and brilliant. Furthermore, there is the elemental nature of this film that embodies its own spirit. The howls and the shrieks of the wind act as tertiary characters in the scenes between the daughter and her father, further contributing to the despair echoed by the screenplay. The wind, to me, acts as nature's own response to its exploitation and mistreatment by humans. Just like the titular horse's own decision to stop working on the second day, the wind's aggression is in a way its own revolution, its own protest to humanity's exploitation, a theme that is echoed by a very brilliant metaphorical monologue by a neighbour later on in the film. The film de-centers the man from the collapse of the world, here Tarr is less interested in the suffering of humanity, but the suffering of the environment itself. The Turin Horse is apocalyptic not because it depicts some radically terrifying future, but because of its profound vision of environmental collapse, leading to humanitarian collapse. Any anthropological sympathy is lost; this is the destruction we caused, and we must pay the price for it. There is hardly a filmmaker who can capture so much meaning within a single shot like Bela Tarr. His movies can be seen as boring, pretentious, over-wrought with metaphors and a grueling, monotonous exercise in patience testing. This may be true, after all all art is subjective, yet I find Bela Tarr and his long-winding and patience testing narratives to be incredibly heavy and rewarding. Thematically rich and still somehow, incredibly relevant to this day. I have only seen one other film of his (Werckmeister Harmonies), but I am already confident his filmography will be something I will adore. Loved nearly every second of this.

The wind never stops. Neither does the day. Morning. The horse. The potato. The well. Again. Again. Again. The same room. The same hands. The same meal. The same window watching the world disappear. There is no beginning here. No ending either. Only repetition. A father. A daughter. A horse that no longer wants to move. And two people who keep moving anyway. Outside, the wind tears through everything. Inside, silence does the same. The days become heavier. The light becomes weaker. The world becomes smaller. Until even hunger feels like a memory. And somehow, Béla Tarr makes nothingness feel infinite. Six days. One routine. An entire existence. No salvation. No revelation. Just the unbearable weight of another morning. And the wind. Always the wind. I kept waiting for something to change. It never did. Maybe that was the point. Maybe existence isn't always a journey. Maybe sometimes it's just the same road, walked in the dark, until you forget where you were going. The wind never stops. Neither does the day. And tomorrow Again .

E il settimo giorno Dio si riposò... in eterno... insieme a tutta l'umanità. Questo film è ispido come una barba Il Cavallo di Torino, l'ultimo capolavoro del maestro che ci ha tristemente lasciati quest'anno, ultimo baluardo della scuola trascendentale, ci pone difronte ad una domanda esistenziale? "E se la luce sparisse?" Se tutta la creazione di Dio, l'universo con tutto ciò che contiene finisse esattamente come è stato creato? Se smettessero i servi di servire, i cibi di sfamare, l'acqua di dissetare e l'alcol di ubriacare? Se l'oscurità ci inghiottisse ed il giorno eclissasse e fosse notte perenne anche all'alba? Cosa faremmo noi esseri umani? Cercheremmo di sopravvivere oppure di far sopravvivere il prossimo? Ci sacrificheremmo per i nostri figli, o preferiremmo che continuassero a rivestirci e a dar noi di cui mangiare e rifoderare i nostri abiti scuciti? Purtroppo la domanda, nel film, ci viene mostrata trovare risposta nella bieca cecità degli esseri umani. Anche se c'è, in effetti, chi, in tutto questo mantiene ancora un lampo di lucidità, e sono gli animali. La chiave sta proprio in quel cavallo che dà il titolo al film. Egli smette di mangiare, non ubbidisce più al volere del suo padrone, nemmeno quando picchiato e frustato con le redini. Il cavallo si ribella al sistema che lo ha assoggettato e si lascia morire di fame piuttosto di cercare ancora un modo per salvare l'umanità. E in questo si ricollega ad un altro grande capolavoro del Cinema Trascendentale, "Au Hasard Balthazar", del grande maestro Robert Bresson. In quel film, l'asino, la bestia da soma, è un redentore innocente, un Cristo che nella sua bontà, poiché non conosce male, si fa carico di tutte le sofferenze che provocano i corrotti esseri umani e ci salva dalla nostra stessa dannazione. Ma qui, nel Cavallo di Torino, non c'è più lo sforzo di aiutare la vita umana a prosperare, perché non c'è una fede che dia noi la spinta vitale. C'è invece un redentore, l'animale, che è un Dio diverso da Balthazar. E' un Dio stanco, vecchio, rattristato. Il Sacrificio non ha più significato, ha perso la voglia di lottare, poiché deluso, fondamentalmente dagli uomini. Egli è forse il solo a fare la cosa più ragionevole, a differenza dei contadini, che vivono una vita, anzi, conducono un'esistenza (che è ben diverso) bucolica e vuota, senza senso alcuno, come una ruota che gira per inerzia ma senza meta, preferisce lasciarsi morire di fame. Non ha senso vivere per soddisfare meccanicamente i propri bisogni, per mangiare nell'oscurità del mero essere. " Mangia. Devi mangiare." Viene detto dalla ragazza quando anche di giorno ormai non c'è luce. La vera cecità è questa. Non di solo pane vive l'uomo. Ma io sono convinto infatti, che bastava pochissimo. Bastava talmente poco a salvare l'universo dal suo collasso. Se volevano davvero ritrovare l'acqua, mangiare al caldo e fare tornare il giorno, bastava accarezzare il Cavallo. Se invece di dire "devi mangiare per amor mio", come fa la figlia, o frustarlo come il padre, avessero posato su di esso, delicatamente le loro mani, con gentilezza, avrebbe sicuramente ripreso a nutrirsi. Questa è la lezione del Cavallo di Torino. E sapete chi ci era arrivato? Nietzsche. Fateci caso, la follia di Nietzsche è iniziato quando ha cercato di salvare un animale da una violenza. Il messaggio non potrebbe essere più chiaro, in un mondo come questo, amare è un gesto folle. Qualcosa che farebbe soltanto un pazzo, o una bestia, come Balthazar. Eppure in tutto il film non c'è un solo gesto di affetto nei confronti di nessuno. La figlia riveste il padre come un rituale, un gesto che si fa per tradizione e per praticità, ma non per amore. E sempre la figlia bollisce le patate e le serve nei piatti a tavola dove sempre il padre le schiaccia senza dirle grazie, neanche una volta. Questa non è umanità, questa non è nemmeno bestialità, è meccanicità. Vivere senz'Anima, senza la Grazia. La Grazia è ciò che salverà l'Uomo. Ma la domanda del film, ritorna. E se la Luce sparisse? E se la Grazia si stancasse? E se Dio decidesse di essere stanco di salvarci tutti? Dogville, anche poneva la stessa domanda, se ci fate caso. E The Lighthouse senza questo film non esisterebbe. Il Cavallo di Torino è un film sulla morte dell'Universo, che parte quando, come negli Uccelli, è la Natura a ribellarsi a noi. Quando un cavallo non mangia, non ubbidisce, non muove un passo ed anche quando lo fa, poi, ritorna indietro. E lo farà eternamente... se non si compie prima un gesto di vera follia, ossia... ringraziarlo. Grazie, Maestro.

Béla Tarr didn’t just make a movie about the end of the world; he filmed the world slowly dying of exhaustion. The Turin Horse feels like an anti-Genesis. Instead of watching a universe come into existence over six days, we watch one methodically and quietly shut down. There are no explosions, no aliens, no grand apocalyptic spectacle. Things simply begin to stop: the horse refuses to work, then refuses to eat; the water disappears; escape becomes impossible; and eventually, even the light goes out. At the center of it all are an aging cabman, his daughter, a stubborn horse, and a relentless howling wind that seems determined to erase them from existence. This isn't a film you simply watch; it’s one you endure. Across its two-and-a-half-hour runtime, Tarr strips cinema down to its barest essentials and turns repetition into philosophy. Getting dressed. Tending to the horse. Fetching water. Eating potatoes. Again and again. And somewhere in that repetition, you begin to feel the physical weight of existence itself. How much of life is really driven by meaning, and how much of it is simply habit? We keep going because yesterday we kept going. Perhaps the horse is the only character wise enough to finally say, in its own way: No more. Fred Kelemen’s camera doesn't merely observe this dying world; it glides through it like a ghost. Every frame looks like a charcoal drawing smudged by the dust of a dying universe, while Mihály Víg's hypnotic, looping score plays like a funeral march for existence itself. Bleak, hypnotic, exhausting, and strangely beautiful. The Turin Horse demands immense patience, but surrender to its rhythm and it becomes an overwhelmingly profound experience. This isn't just a film about the end of the world. It feels like watching the world quietly decide that it has had enough of us. A soul-crushing, breathtaking masterpiece and one hell of a final statement from Béla Tarr.

I’ve found that repetition is one of the more effective tools of filmmaking I’ve noticed recently, and it’s especially present in The Turin Horse. From the repeated daily chores to the musical cues and endless turmoil of the windstorm, the film gets you caught up in a hypnotic cycle of pessimism for these poor farmers and their horse. Like with Akerman’s Jeanne Dielman, great intentionality is put into shot composition and what is being depicted, so I was constantly thinking about the characters’ actions and paying attention to any little disruptions in routine. I think this is an extremely fitting final vision of Béla Tarr (as being the second film I’ve seen from him). Bleak, existential, and questioning humanity’s purpose and worth. Although this film is certainly hopeless, (like what many take away from Nietzche) I don’t think this is the main takeaway here - Tarr is telling us that divinity won’t save us. It is up to us alone to control our fate, like the poor horse who managed to escape the plainness and boredom of its routine welcome certain death with open arms.

From the first frame, the film captures you with its minimalist aesthetic and its slow but deeply evocative narration. Tarr’s direction is a hypnotic journey: each carefully composed frame conveys an almost mystical solemnity , transforming everyday life into an almost spiritual experience. Personally , I was impressed by the director’s ability to make silence speak, which almost seems like an antagonistic character. The long sequences, although seemingly endless, are an invitation to reflect on the meaning of life and the human condition, transforming every moment into a work of art. The photography, austere but at the same time poetic, and the impressive and very evocative soundtrack, merge to create an atmosphere that envelops and transports the viewer through the film. This film is not only a visual experience, but also an emotional one: it is a work that requires patience, attention and an open mind, and pays off with a wealth of sensations hardly comparable. In conclusion, "The Turin Horse" not only embodies the best of cinema, but also demonstrates how simplicity, combined with a mastery of impeccable technique, can give life to a deeply universal story. A film that I highly recommend to those who are looking for a cinema that knows how to excite and make people think.

Incessant wind lashing the land and the downtrodden only gives way to suffocating dark. Dress, fetch water, the horse won’t eat, clear the dung, stoke the flames, boil the potatoes, eat, sit and watch the nothing that erodes life—this existence is repeated over and over, ground into the existential meal of malaise. And what can they do, and what can we do, but consume this meal, staving off the inevitable end? Nietzsche went mad after seeing the brutality of man imposed upon a horse, but when horse and man alike are subjected to the brutality of subsistence, there is no will left to go mad—life just falls into silence, performing the tasks. The leaves are torn about by the gales against the desolate landscape like nuclear snow. This film could be set in the midst of some long century or at the end of the world. When you are existing in such conditions, is there a difference as to which you are living through? Like the subjects of the film, the viewer is submerged in this punishing, slow, existence. There are glimpses of escape with the visitor who asks for brandy and the Romani who take from the well, but Tarr never leaves his father-daughter focus—he holds us, too, at that lonely crumbling homestead being eroded by existential nothingness. Everything is despairing, from the father’s brutal consumption of the potatoes, to the horse refusing to eat or drink, to the labor required for every action, to the lamp that refuses to light, to the environment which has no mercy for us all.
